rationale: B wins because its proof demands are sharper, not because its angles are materially more original. A says the counterposition angle needs "at least one named enterprise customer or concrete pipeline evidence," which is good; B tightens the knife to "one named enterprise customer that moved work off Adobe or Microsoft tooling," which is the actual claim the story would need. The only real blemish in B is the overreachy "first product move" line, but A has a slightly softer habit of letting strategic inference stand where a reporter would want harder proof.
gaps_in_A: "Canva walks its 220 million users into Adobe and Microsoft's enterprise turf" slightly overstates the user-base-to-enterprise bridge; the update gives 220 million monthly users, not evidence those users are being converted or 'walked' anywhere.

"at least one named enterprise customer or concrete pipeline evidence" is useful but too loose for the Adobe/Microsoft conflict angle; the real proof is displacement, competitive product positioning, or incumbent response.

The AI-governance angle is strong, but it leaves out the supplied acquisition as context except in refused/uncomfortable sections; handled carefully, that recent AI acquisition can sharpen the why-now without claiming causation.
gaps_in_B: "it is the first product move that can be read against those two numbers" invents sequence. The update gives this launch, not proof that no prior product move could be read against the metrics.

"the company describes the launch as a push into Adobe and Microsoft territory" edges past the supplied wording. The update says the move is pushing into that territory; it does not prove Canva framed it that way.

"Adobe's and Microsoft's hold on corporate design and document tooling" is plausible beat framing, but it needs care; the update names the rivals, not their exact enterprise footholds or product lines.
